title: Thinking Slowly About Loss Aversion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Written on the occasion of Daniel Kahneman's death, this article revisits the Nobel laureate's core insight about loss aversion: people feel the pain of a loss roughly twice as intensely as the pleasure of an equivalent gain. The piece connects this bias to everyday behaviors, from golfers who make more putts for par than birdie to consumers over-purchasing insurance, and extends it to leadership contexts like staying too long in a role or over-indexing on risk avoidance instead of pursuing breakthroughs. It closes by suggesting that consciously reframing decisions around opportunity and growth, rather than risk and loss, is a deliberate practice good decision-makers cultivate.
points: Daniel Kahneman's research showed people feel losses roughly twice as intensely as equivalent gains.
Loss aversion explains behaviors like better par putts than birdie putts and over-purchasing insurance.
The bias also explains why people stay too long in unhealthy relationships or unfulfilling roles.
Leaders often over-focus on avoiding risk rather than pursuing growth because of this bias.
Deliberately reframing decisions around opportunity rather than loss can counteract the effect.
quotes: Nobel prize-winning behavioral economist Daniel Kahneman passed away at the age of 90 a few days ago.
Fast thinking is emotional, while slow thinking is analytical.
Kahneman found that people experience more psychological pain from losses than they do pleasure from equivalent gains.
This is why golfers make more putts for par than for birdie, why tennis players rarely miss the second serve, and why consumers are more likely to purchase unnecessary insurance and warranties.
Because of the loss aversion bias, people overestimate the probability of negative events happening.
Emphasizing opportunities, gains, and growth, as opposed to risks and potential loss, is a mindset good decision-makers develop on purpose.
